column1: # G4 phase 1: id(name) -- the IDENTITY MARK
# that the enclosing value is an independent ENTITY named `name`, and
# EVERY node in one evaluation carrying that name is unified with every
# other. Declaring two nodes the same entity MEANS unifying them, so a
# contradiction between them is an ordinary located conflict -- the
# anti-`owl:sameAs`, where full-substitutability identity links with no
# conflict detection produced silent corruption at web scale.
# The tree stays a TREE. After merging, every declared position holds
# the merged value and generation emits it at each path -- duplication,
# exactly as references generate today. Identity adds a
# location-independent addressing scheme; it does not change the shape
# of the output, and no value is ever shared or aliased.
# The design's own worked example is `merge-nested-paths`: two files
# describing one service at different tree paths used to evaluate
# together in silence, because unification is path-aligned and `tier:1`
# and `tier:2` were never brought into contact. With an id on both,

column3: catalog: payments: id(svc_payments) & {owner:"team-pay"}\ndeploy: eu1: payments: id(svc_payments) & {replicas:3}

column1: # A name is letters, digits, `_`, `-`, `/` -- and NO DOTS, because a dot
# separates an entity address from a path inside that entity (G4 phase
# 2), so a dotted id would make `svc_auth.port` ambiguous. A `-` must be
# quoted: `-` is not a bare-text character (op-chars.tsv pins `a:6-2` as
# a parse error), while `/` parses as plain text and may stay bare.
# A contradiction between two positions of one entity is NOT a code of
# its own: it is the ordinary conflict of whatever disagreed, at the
# site that disagreed. That is the whole point of merging by
# unification rather than by copying. `id_conflict` is reserved for the
# different failure of two NAMES on one node.
# A CONSTANT id() inside an `&:` template would declare every child of
# the bag to be one entity, and the merge would then unify all of them
# together. Refused at parse, so the refusal reaches every child AND the
# bag itself -- which is what makes an empty bag with a bad template an
# error too. Canon renders the refusal as a nil in the tree, exactly as
# it renders a bad arity or an unknown function; generation reports it.
# The escape hatch is a PATH-DEPENDENT name, and for a map template
# applied at the child position that is `key(0)` -- the child's own key.
# Plain `key()` reads one level UP (func.tsv, `key-one`), so in a
# template it names the BAG, and every child collides on that one name.
# That is a defined result rather than a refusal: rule 3 is a syntactic
# guard on constants, and no parse-time check can know what a computed
# --- Clearing rules 1 and 2: references and copy() --------------------
# A reference's clone and a copy() are COPIES of an entity, not the
# `ref-and-merge` in ref.tsv) would push `y:2` back into `q.a` through
# the merge, silently changing pinned behaviour, and copy() would be a
# no-op for exactly the values it exists to detach.
# Canon renders the identity back as the conjunct an author writes, so
# it reparses to the same entity, and the merge is idempotent on
# re-read. This deliberately differs from the type/hide MARKS, which
# canon drops (marks.tsv, `type-canon`): identity is semantic content,
# and G6's canon-hash must see it -- two documents that disagree about
# which entity a node IS do not mean the same thing.
# --- Riders together, and what the merge carries ---------------------
# The identity and the deprecation record are both riders on the value,
# and canon nests them in a fixed order. `merge-hide-covers-every-
# position` records a consequence worth knowing: a mark on ONE
# declaration of an entity reaches every position of it, because every
# position holds the one merged value. Hiding a declaration hides the
# Five columns, as why.tsv describes. The merge is a MEET like any
# other, so it is recorded like any other: a field a position picked up
# from ANOTHER declaration of the same entity names the site that wrote
# it, and a position that agrees with its twin names both. Aligning the
# two ports here moved the canonical implementation twice — a
# peer-only key is now met rather than carried under instrumentation,
# and the equal-pair fast path is skipped there — because the Go
# recorder wraps the whole dispatcher and TypeScript's sat at the tail
# of the slow path. Uninstrumented runs are untouched.
# BARE id() IS NAMED BY THE ENCLOSING KEY (RELATIONS.0.md §3.1),
# late-bound: the name is taken where the value LANDS, per ADR-009's
# key() rule. This is the primitive the broken id(key(0)) idiom wanted
# (use-cases/10-data-model gap 6). At the document root there is no
# enclosing key to be named by.
# In a spread template each child takes its OWN key -- the shape the
# constant-id refusal (id_spread) exists to force, now expressible

column3: t: {&: id() & {kind: string}, a: {kind: k1}, b: {kind: k2}}

column1: # THE SCHEMA IDIOM: a type body carrying bare id(), spread over data.
# The one-pass defer is what makes this work -- the pass-zero snapshot
# takes the body with the id() still open, so each child resolves at
# its own key (the graph rows in graph.tsv pin the entity sets).

column3: S: type(id() & {kind: string})\nsvcs: {&: $.S, payments: {kind: pay}, ledger: {kind: led}}

column1: # A plain reference COPIES, and a copy is not the entity (clearing
# rule 1) -- the values flow, the identity does not.
# D-1 NAME GRAMMAR (RELATIONS.0.md): a flat identifier -- no slash, no
# leading digit or hyphen. The quoted spellings, since a bare 9x is
# lexable but a bare -x is an operator.
# A LIST element's enclosing "key" is its index, and an index is not a
# D-1 name -- the same rule as the document root: nothing to be named
# AN ENTITY CANNOT CONTAIN ITSELF. Identity merge unifies every node
# carrying a name with every other node carrying it, so naming a node
# AND ITS OWN DESCENDANT the same entity asks for a value that contains
# itself. Both engines used to build it and die on the HOST stack:
# TypeScript with a bare "Maximum call stack size exceeded" carrying no
# `[aontu/...]` marker for a harness to see, and Go with a `fatal
# error: stack overflow` -- which is not recoverable, so an embedding
# server could not defend against a 22-character document. The refusal
# was the only missing piece; the merge had both sites in hand all
# The refusal lands on the DESCENDANT, the position that cannot stand.
# THE BOUNDARY IS EXACTLY ANCESTOR-TO-DESCENDANT, and these are the
# adjacent spellings that must keep working -- two of them are the
# feature itself, which is why the refusal has to be this narrow.
